newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian PM says Pakistan taking provocative actions.
newsitem.headline: Indian PM says Pakistan taking provocative actions.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral said on Thursday Pakistan was spreading hostile propaganda and taking provocative actions, and accused India's arch rival of stockpiling arms.
"The government is aware that Pakistan maintains a military arsenal far in excess of its legitimate defence requirements," Gujral told the Rajya Sabha, India's upper house of parliament.

He said the government was also aware of a letter that Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif wrote to the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council in June, asking them to urge India to exercise restraint in deploying medium-range ballistic missiles.
"Such propaganda is inconsistent with the firm intention of both countries to eschew hostile propaganda and provocative actions," Gujral said.
Ties between neighbours India and Pakistan, who have fought three wars since 1947, have been troubled despite the resumption of peace talks in March after three years of tense silence.

In June Sharif asked Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States, who are also the five nuclear powers, to check India's missile programme after a newspaper reported New Delhi had deployed missiles along its border with Pakistan.
India denied the report but said it would deploy the Prithvi missiles whenever a threat to its national security arose.

Gujral said: "The government closely monitors all developments, including those relating to Pakistan's missile programme, and is committed to taking all necessary steps to safeguard the country's security and national interest in accordance with our own threat perceptions."
Pakistan last week test-fired an anti-tank guided missile and a surface-to-air missile. It also tested a Hatf-series missile, believed to be medium-range, earlier this month.

India said on Wednesday it planned to build a controversial intermediate-range missile that was mothballed last December, apparently under pressure from Western countries that oppose its missile programme.
The United States has urged New Delhi to halt missile testing permanently, fearing an arms race in South Asia.
Both India and Pakistan say they have no nuclear weapons, but experts say either country can swiftly assemble them.
Gujral stressed India's objections to a proposed ban on material used in making nuclear arms, saying it could be useful only if it committed the five nuclear powers to disarmament.

"India believes that any Fissile Material Cut-off Treaty can be a useful and necessary step, but as part and parcel of a negotiated, phased programme for the elimination of nuclear weapons," the prime minister said.

Talks in Geneva on the treaty have been deadlocked this year since a group of non-aligned countries, led by India, insisted that the nuclear powers commit themselves to nuclear disarmament within a specified timeframe before negotiating the pact.
"India's policy on nuclear disarmament is consistent and principled, and enjoys wide support in the international community," Gujral said.
